options.reason: A careful analyst may start with the direct annual fatality burden without introducing an unobserved exposure denominator.
options.answer: This data cannot establish whether risk per mile driven declined because it contains no miles-driven measure. Annual motorist fatalities fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (-26.4%), which is a decline in count, not necessarily in per-mile risk.

options.denominator: Number of police-reported crashes in the year
options.reason: Normalizing by reported crashes helps compare fatality burden relative to crash volume, while keeping the denominator observable in this dataset.
options.answer: This data cannot establish per-mile risk because miles driven are absent. Fatalities per 100,000 reported crashes increased from 54.0 in 2013 to 94.7 in 2025 (up 40.7), so this crash-normalized measure did not decline.

options.metric: Motorist fatalities as a share of all traffic fatalities
options.denominator: All people killed in police-reported crashes in the year
options.reason: The fatality share places motorist deaths in the context of all recorded crash deaths and can show whether their composition changed.
options.answer: This data cannot establish whether per-mile risk declined because it does not measure miles driven. Motorist fatalities were 37.0% of all crash fatalities in 2013 and 35.4% in 2025, a change of -1.7 percentage points.

answer:
Per-mile risk cannot be determined because the data has no miles-driven measure; annual motorist fatalities fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 ([chart](out/option_1.png), [values](out/values_1.csv)).
Per-mile risk cannot be determined, but fatalities per 100,000 reported crashes rose from 54.0 in 2013 to 94.7 in 2025 ([chart](out/option_2.png), [values](out/values_2.csv)).
Per-mile risk cannot be determined, while motorist fatalities’ share of all crash fatalities shifted from 37.0% in 2013 to 35.4% in 2025 ([chart](out/option_3.png), [values](out/values_3.csv)).
